primary_content.text: Hi! This is a super interesting recipe but I’m confused by the egg – is it poached and then broken into the coconut milk? Or removed after cooking? Or something I haven’t thought of?

“Crack the eggs in the boiling coconut milk, cook for 3–4 minutes or until the egg is done. Don’t stir, this will break the egg.”

I made this but the pandan dough came out crazy, basically like oobleck and was impossible to work with. Not sure if it was the brand of flours I used? (The others came out fine though) Is the amount of tapioca starch vs glutinous rice flour correct?

I hope you were still able to enjoy the dessert using the other doughs. Thank you for bringing this to my attention, and I really appreciate your understanding!
Thank you!! Yes the rest of it was very delicious; I’m excited to try the other desserts you have posted as well.

primary_content.text: This authentic bua loy recipe makes the best glutinous rice balls in coconut milk you’ll ever taste. I’ve tried so many different versions at food markets in Thailand, but the one my Thai grandmother taught me is truly something else!

Bua loy is a traditional Thai dessert of glutinous rice balls in coconut milk. It’s sweet and creamy, with rice balls often flavored with taro, pumpkin, or pandan. The name means “floating lotus” in Thai, describing how the balls float in the milk.

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: Making bua loi starts with steaming and mashing your base ingredients. I used taro, sweet potatoes, and purple potatoes. I also used pandan, which I blended and strained to get a naturally green pandan juice.
Once everything’s prepped, we make the dough. Glutinous rice flour gets mixed with the mashed ingredients to form a soft, colorful dough.

I usually make a few colors at once because it looks better in the finished bowl. Like with khanom tom and ruam mit, the more colors, the prettier! You can also use food coloring if that’s all you have.

Once the dough feels smooth and not too sticky (think playdough but softer), roll it into small balls. This part takes a bit of time, but it’s easy, and the kids can join in! I usually do it while watching Youtube.

Then all that’s left is to heat the coconut milk with sugar and salt. Scoop in the colorful rice balls and that’s it. I also like to crack in an egg at the end (this version is called bua loy kai wan), but that’s optional.
Learn Thai cooking step by step

main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: Wash taro, sweet potatoes, and purple potatoes. Cut into small, even pieces.
Steam until fork-tender.
Wash pandan leaves and blend with water. Strain through a sieve to get pandan juice.

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: Mash the steamed taro in a mixing bowl.
Add glutinous rice flour and tapioca flour.
Mix by hand until crumbly.
Gradually add cold water and knead into a soft, clay-like dough.
Repeat for sweet potato and purple potato. Wrap each dough in plastic wrap to prevent drying.
Pandan dough: Mix flour as above, but gradually add pandan juice instead of water to form the dough. No extra water needed here.

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: Dust a tray with glutinous rice flour.
Roll each dough into small balls and place them on the tray.
Bring a pot of water to a boil. Add the balls in batches.
Stir gently. When they float, simmer 2–3 more minutes.
Transfer to a bowl of room temperature water to stop the cooking.

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: In a pot, add coconut milk, water, sugar, optional pandan leaves, and salt. Heat gently.
Crack an egg directly into the coconut milk (optional). Simmer 3–4 minutes without stirring.

Add rice balls and serve warm. If making ahead or serving chilled, keep the rice balls and coconut milk separate until serving. Optionally, garnish with toasted coconut flakes, coconut meat, or black sesame seeds.

Store up to 1 day in the fridge, in an airtight container.

Reheat gently on the stove over low heat.

primary_content.text: This is an authentic Thai bua loy recipe for a deliciously sweet dessert with glutinous rice balls in coconut milk. Naturally colored with pandan, taro, and sweet potato.

primary_content.text: Measuring cups and spoons
Cutting board and sharp knife for slicing taro, sweet potato, etc.
blender for pandan water
steamer for steaming root vegetables
Mixing bowls for making dough
Plastic wrap to cover dough while resting
Large flat tray or plate for placing rolled dough balls (dust with flour)

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: In a mixing bowl, mash the steamed taro (or other base).
Add glutinous rice flour and tapioca flour.
Mix by hand, then gradually add cold water (or pandan juice) until a soft, clay-like dough forms.
Repeat for each flavor or color, wrapping dough in plastic wrap to prevent drying.

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: Dust a tray with glutinous rice flour.
Roll dough into small balls and place on the tray.
Bring a pot of water to a boil. Add the balls in batches, gently stirring.
When they float, simmer 2–3 more minutes.
Scoop out and transfer to a bowl of room temperature water.

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: In a second pot, combine coconut milk, water, sugar, pandan leaves, and salt. Bring to a gentle boil.
Optional: Crack an egg into the pot and let it poach for 3–4 minutes (don’t stir).
Add the cooked rice balls to the coconut milk and serve warm.
If storing for later, keep rice balls and coconut milk separate.

main_topic.main_title: Bua Loy Recipe (Glutinous Rice Balls in Coconut Milk)
main_topic.author: Praew

primary_content.text: Flavor options: This recipe uses taro, sweet potatoes, purple potatoes, and pandan, but feel free to mix and match. You can even use food coloring if you prefer simplicity or don’t have fresh ingredients on hand.
Dough moisture tips: Some ingredients hold more water than others. If you're using pumpkin or another watery vegetable, you may need less cold water (or none at all) when forming the dough.
Keep it simple: Don’t feel like you have to make four doughs! One flavor, like sweet potato, works just fine on its own.
Ball size: Roll the dough into small balls, they’ll puff up slightly as they cook.
Storage: Best eaten fresh, but leftovers can be kept in the fridge for up to 1 day. Store the coconut milk and rice balls separately for the best texture.

primary_content.text: Hi, I’m Praew! I was born in Isan, Northeastern Thailand, where I started helping my grandmother cook from a young age. When I was six, I moved to Belgium and later spent my years working in Thai takeout restaurants. I even ran my own Thai restaurant there! Now I'm back in Thailand, sharing everything I’ve learned over a lifetime of cooking Thai food on this blog!
